chapter_summary:
While the CPU handles the game's logic, the GPU is responsible for drawing everything you see on screen. When your game is GPU-bound, it means the graphics card is struggling to render all the visual elements fast enough, resulting in a low frame rate. Optimizing GPU usage is critical for visually rich games and especially important for target platforms with limited graphical power, like mobile devices.

One of the most significant factors affecting GPU performance is the number of **draw calls**. A draw call is an instruction from the CPU to the GPU to render a batch of triangles. Each draw call has an overhead, and if you have thousands of individual draw calls per frame, the CPU can become a bottleneck just trying to tell the GPU what to do, even if the GPU itself isn't overwhelmed by the rendering complexity. Unity offers several techniques to reduce draw calls:

*   **Batching:** This is the process of combining multiple meshes into a single mesh before sending them to the GPU, thereby reducing the number of draw calls.
    *   **Static Batching:** For GameObjects marked as "Static" in the Inspector (under the `Static` dropdown menu), Unity can combine their meshes into large batches at editor time. This is highly effective for stationary environmental objects.
    *   **Dynamic Batching:** For smaller, non-static meshes that share the same material, Unity can dynamically batch them at runtime. There are limitations: objects must have fewer than 300 vertices, use the same material, and not have complex shader features.
    *   **GPU Instancing:** A more advanced technique, primarily for objects that share the same mesh and material but have different transformations (position, rotation, scale). It allows the GPU to render many copies of the same mesh in a single draw call, passing the transformation data efficiently. This is excellent for large armies of identical units or fields of grass. To enable GPU Instancing, ensure your material's shader supports it (Standard Shader does) and check the "Enable Instancing" checkbox on the material.

Another powerful optimization is **Level of Detail (LOD)**. LOD groups allow you to define multiple versions of a mesh, each with varying levels of detail (e.g., high-poly, medium-poly, low-poly). As the camera moves further away from an object, Unity automatically switches to a lower-detail mesh, reducing the number of triangles the GPU needs to render. This is particularly effective for complex models in open-world games. You can create an LOD Group component (`Component > Rendering > LOD Group`) and drag different mesh versions into its slots, defining the screen percentage at which each LOD level becomes active.

```csharp
// Example of how LODs work conceptually, not direct code
// Unity handles LOD switching automatically via the LOD Group component.
// You would create multiple mesh assets (e.g., MyTree_LOD0, MyTree_LOD1, MyTree_LOD2)
// and assign them to an LOD Group component on your GameObject.
```

**Occlusion Culling** is a technique that prevents Unity from rendering objects that are completely hidden by other objects (occluders) from the camera's perspective. Unlike frustum culling (which Unity does automatically for objects outside the camera's view), occlusion culling requires baking the scene's visibility data. To use it, mark your static environment objects as "Occluder Static" and "Occludee Static" in the Inspector, then open the Occlusion Culling window (`Window > Rendering > Occlusion Culling`) and click "Bake." This can significantly reduce the number of triangles processed by the GPU in complex indoor or urban environments.

Optimizing **textures and materials** is also crucial.
*   **Texture Atlasing:** Combine multiple small textures into a single, larger texture atlas. This allows multiple objects to share the same material and texture, making them eligible for batching and reducing draw calls.
*   **Texture Compression:** Use appropriate compression formats (e.g., DXT for desktop, ETC/PVRTC for mobile) and lower resolutions where possible. Access texture import settings by selecting a texture in the Project window.
*   **Shader Complexity:** Complex shaders with many passes, expensive calculations, or multiple texture lookups can be very demanding on the GPU. Use simpler shaders (e.g., Unlit, Mobile/Diffuse) for less critical objects, and avoid unnecessary features. The Frame Debugger (`Window > Analysis > Frame Debugger`) can help you analyze individual draw calls and their associated shader complexity.

Finally, be mindful of **lighting and post-processing effects**. Real-time lights, especially those with shadows, are very expensive. Use baked lighting (`Window > Rendering > Lighting > Settings`) for static lights whenever possible. Limit the number of real-time lights, especially directional and point lights. Post-processing effects like Bloom, Depth of Field, and Anti-aliasing add significant overhead. Use them judiciously and test their performance impact on your target hardware. For example, using a simpler, faster anti-aliasing solution like FXAA instead of MSAA might be necessary on mobile.

By combining these techniques, you can significantly reduce the workload on your GPU, leading to higher frame rates and a smoother visual experience for your players. Always remember to profile your changes to confirm their positive impact.

screens.title: GPU & Rendering Optimization
screens.subtitle: Make rendering efficient: fewer draw calls, smarter LODs, and budgeted lighting

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn why the G P U often becomes the limiting factor for frame rate and how to relieve that pressure. We will define draw calls and show three practical draw-call reduction techniques: static batching, dynamic batching, and G P U instancing. You will also learn how Level of Detail groups reduce triangle counts as objects recede, and how occlusion culling prevents the engine from drawing things the player cannot see. Texture atlasing, careful compression, and simpler shader choices will be covered to reduce texture bandwidth and shader cost. Finally, we consider lighting and post-processing costs and when to bake or simplify effects. Each topic includes concrete steps you can apply in Unity, and a hands-on lab walks through creating LOD groups and marking objects as static to observe draw call reductions with the Frame Debugger. By the end, you will know which techniques to apply in different scenarios and how to verify improvements with profiling. Consider which optimization would help your current project most: reduce draw calls, lower geometry, or cut shader complexity?

keyIdea.title: Optimize what you draw
keyIdea.text: Reducing draw calls, simplifying shaders, and avoiding work on unseen geometry are the fastest ways to lower GPU load and raise frame rate.

screens.title: What is a Draw Call?
screens.subtitle: Define the unit of rendering work and its cost

narration.text: A draw call is the basic instruction the C P U sends to the G P U to render geometry. It includes which mesh to draw, what material and shader to use, and transformation data. Each draw call carries C P U overhead: setting G P U state, binding buffers, and issuing the command. When you have thousands of distinct draw calls per frame, the C P U spends a lot of time just telling the G P U what to do, and that can become the bottleneck even if the G P U could handle the geometry. A concrete example: a forest made of many unique objects with separate materials can generate thousands of draw calls. The solution is to reduce the number of times you switch materials and bind new meshes. A common misconception is that triangle count alone determines performance. While triangles matter, draw-call overhead can dominate on scenes with many small objects. Key takeaway: measure if your frame time shows high C P U time in the render loop; if it does, focus on draw-call reduction strategies first. How many draw calls does your scene average when you profile it?

keyIdea.title: Draw call = CPU-to-GPU command
keyIdea.text: Reducing the number of draw calls cuts CPU overhead and often yields immediate frame-rate gains.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › What is a Draw Call?
Definition
Draw call explained

A draw call is the command from CPU to GPU that binds geometry, materials, and issues the render. Each call has fixed CPU cost for state changes and dispatch. High counts increase CPU frame time.

Bullets
  • Includes mesh, material, shader, and transform data.
  • Has CPU overhead for state changes and buffer bindings.
  • Thousands of small draw calls often mean CPU-bound rendering.
Key Takeaway

If the render thread is heavy in the profiler, focus first on reducing draw calls before more costly GPU-side changes.

Concrete Example
Imagine a scene with 2,000 identical rocks, each with its own mesh and material. Without batching, that's 2,000 draw calls. With instancing or batching, you can render them with a handful of draw calls, greatly reducing CPU overhead.
Common misconception
Many assume reducing triangles is always the best fix. In practice, if the CPU spends most time issuing draw calls, reducing draw calls yields larger gains than modest triangle cuts.
Check your understanding
Action
Profile the render thread and note draw-call count.
Question
Is the CPU or GPU the bottleneck?

screens.title: Static Batching
screens.subtitle: Combine static geometry at edit time to lower draw calls

narration.text: Static batching combines meshes marked as static into larger meshes at build or editor time so they can be drawn with fewer draw calls. It is ideal for stationary environmental items like buildings, rocks, and props that never move relative to the scene. To use it, mark objects as Static in the Inspector and ensure the Batching Static flag is enabled. Unity merges compatible meshes into larger batches when you enter play or build, reducing per-object draw calls. One concrete example is an urban scene with many lampposts and crates: marking them static can change hundreds of individual draw calls into a handful. A common concern is memory usage: static batching can increase R A M because combined meshes duplicate vertex data. Measure both draw calls and memory usage in the profiler to ensure the trade-off is acceptable for your target platform. Key takeaway: use static batching for many identical or similar immobile objects to reduce C P U overhead and improve frame rates, but watch memory on constrained devices. Static Batching means static batching reduces draw calls for immobile objects, trading runtime draw calls for increased baked mesh memory usage.. In practical terms, combine static geometry at edit time to lower draw calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Batch at edit time
keyIdea.text: Static batching reduces draw calls for immobile objects, trading runtime draw calls for increased baked mesh memory usage.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Static Batching
Process
How static batching works
  1. Mark immobile GameObjects as Static / Batching Static in the Inspector.
  2. During build or play, Unity combines compatible meshes into larger meshes.
  3. The combined meshes are sent as fewer draw calls to the GPU at runtime.
When to use: large numbers of stationary objects that share materials. Watch for increased memory usage from duplicated vertex buffers in combined meshes.
Example
Mark 100 crates as Static and observe how draw calls decrease in the Frame Debugger, often from 100 calls down to a few batches.
Visual Flow
Many Static Objects
→
Combined Mesh
→
Fewer Draw Calls
Common Mistake
Marking animated or moving objects as Static. Static batching assumes immobility; changing transforms will break visuals or not be batched.

screens.title: Dynamic Batching
screens.subtitle: Reduce draw calls for small, similar moving objects

narration.text: Dynamic batching combines small meshes at runtime when they share the same material. It is best suited to objects with very low vertex counts — Unity typically requires fewer than 300 vertices per object — and with simple shaders. The engine combines their vertex data into a single G P U buffer at runtime, reducing draw calls without baking combined meshes ahead of time. A useful example: many small pickups or bullets that move in the scene. Because dynamic batching happens at runtime, it avoids increased memory from combined meshes, but it has limitations: vertex count thresholds, shared materials, and no complex shader features. A common misconception is that dynamic batching always outperforms instancing. In truth, G P U instancing tends to scale better for many identical objects because it is driven by the G P U and avoids per-frame C P U combining. Key takeaway: enable dynamic batching for small, varied moving objects that share materials, but test performance and compare with instancing for large instance counts. Dynamic Batching means dynamic batching merges small, similar moving meshes during play, useful when static batching isn't applicable.. In practical terms, reduce draw calls for small, similar moving objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Batch at runtime
keyIdea.text: Dynamic batching merges small, similar moving meshes during play, useful when static batching isn't applicable.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Dynamic Batching
Definition
What dynamic batching does
At runtime, Unity can combine small meshes that share a material into a single draw call. It is limited by vertex counts and shader features.
When to use
  • Many small moving objects under vertex limits.
  • Objects that share the same material and simple shaders.
Key Takeaway

Dynamic batching saves draw calls for small objects at runtime without increasing baked mesh memory, but it has strict limits and must be profiled against instancing.

Concrete Example
A swarm of 200 small floating particles that share a simple material can be dynamically batched into fewer draw calls if each particle is under the vertex limit and the shader is simple.
Common Mistake
Expecting dynamic batching to handle high-vertex meshes or complex shaders. If objects exceed the vertex budget, batching will not occur.
Pro tip
If many identical moving objects exist, compare dynamic batching against GPU instancing to see which performs better on your target hardware.

screens.title: GPU Instancing
screens.subtitle: Render many identical meshes efficiently in one draw call

narration.text: G P U instancing lets the G P U draw many copies of the same mesh and material using a single draw call, supplying per-instance transform or parameter data. It's particularly valuable for large counts of identical objects like trees in a field or crowds of units. To use G P U instancing in Unity, ensure the shader supports instancing — the Standard Shader does — and enable 'Enable Instancing' on the material. Unlike batching, instancing avoids duplicating geometry in memory and scales better as instance counts rise because the G P U handles variations efficiently. A concrete example: rendering a field of grass blades as a single instanced draw reduces draw calls dramatically while keeping memory usage modest. A misconception is that instancing always outperforms batching; in small object counts or where objects vary in material, static or dynamic batching can be preferable. Key takeaway: enable instancing for many identical objects with the same material and test with the Frame Debugger to confirm the draw call consolidation. GPU Instancing means instancing delegates repetition to the gpu, reducing cpu draw-call overhead and often scaling better for large sets of identical objects.. In practical terms, render many identical meshes efficiently in one draw call. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Let the GPU repeat work
keyIdea.text: Instancing delegates repetition to the GPU, reducing CPU draw-call overhead and often scaling better for large sets of identical objects.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › GPU Instancing
Definition
How instancing works
A single draw call can tell the GPU to render the same mesh many times with per-instance transform or parameter data. This reduces CPU overhead and avoids duplicating mesh data.
When to use
  • Large numbers of identical meshes that differ only by transform or simple parameters.
  • Materials that support instancing — enable the checkbox on the material.
Key Takeaway

GPU instancing is ideal for many identical objects and often yields better scaling than CPU-side batching for large counts.

Concrete Example
A meadow filled with thousands of identical grass meshes can be drawn as a small number of instanced draw calls, with transform arrays providing position and rotation per instance.
Checklist
  • Confirm shader supports instancing.
  • Enable 'Enable Instancing' on the material.
  • Batch similar instances into one instanced draw when possible.
Contrast
Instancing excels with high instance counts of identical meshes. For a few unique objects, batching or none at all may be simpler.

screens.title: Level of Detail (LOD) Groups
screens.subtitle: Swap meshes by distance to reduce triangle throughput

narration.text: Level of Detail groups allow you to provide multiple mesh versions for the same object and let Unity switch between them based on screen size or camera distance. Typical LOD chains include high, medium, and low polygon meshes. As an object moves further away, a lower-detail mesh is automatically used, greatly reducing the triangles the G P U must rasterize. An example: a tree with LOD0 at five thousand triangles, LOD1 at one thousand polygons, and LOD2 at a few hundred. In a forest, distant trees can be switched to LOD2 without noticeable quality loss, cutting triangle cost dramatically. A misconception is that LOD is only for extreme ranges; in fact, careful transition thresholds yield smooth visual results and big savings even at moderate distances. To implement in Unity, add an LOD Group component and assign meshes to slots, then duplicate many instances and profile the scene. Key takeaway: LODs reduce G P U triangle throughput and are especially effective for complex models in open-world scenes. Level of Detail (LOD) Groups means lod groups trade geometry for distance-aware performance savings with minimal visible impact when configured properly.. In practical terms, swap meshes by distance to reduce triangle throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reduce triangles by distance
keyIdea.text: LOD groups trade geometry for distance-aware performance savings with minimal visible impact when configured properly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › LOD Groups
Definition
What LOD groups do
LOD groups swap mesh complexity based on screen percentage or camera distance, lowering vertex and triangle workload as objects get smaller on screen.
Implementation steps
  1. Create multiple mesh versions for an object.
  2. Add an LOD Group component to the parent GameObject.
  3. Assign mesh renderers for each LOD slot and set transition percentages.
Key Takeaway

LOD groups are essential for complex models in open worlds. Good transition thresholds keep visuals consistent while reducing GPU load.

Concrete Example
Create MyTree_LOD0, _LOD1, and _LOD2. Add them to an LOD Group and duplicate the tree across the landscape. As you move the camera, watch the triangle count drop in the profiler as LODs switch.
Pro tip
Use simple primitives as placeholder LODs while iterating. Tune transition percentages to hide popping and limit the number of LOD levels to what you need.
Misconception
Thinking LODs always reduce draw calls. LODs reduce triangles, but draw-call count depends on material usage and batching. Combine LODs with batching for best results.

screens.title: Occlusion Culling
screens.subtitle: Bake visibility so hidden geometry isn't rendered

narration.text: Occlusion culling prevents rendering of objects that are completely blocked from the camera's view by other geometry. Unity's built-in frustum culling already excludes objects outside the camera cone, but occlusion culling goes further by using precomputed visibility data to skip objects behind walls or large occluders. To use it, mark static environment geometry as Occluder Static and mark potential occludees as Occludee Static. Then open the Occlusion Culling window and click Bake. This generates visibility data that Unity consults at runtime to avoid rendering hidden objects. A concrete example is a complex indoor level: objects in other rooms that the player cannot see are skipped entirely, often slashing triangle counts. A common mistake is relying on occlusion culling for dynamic objects; since the baked data assumes static scene geometry, dynamic items may need alternative runtime solutions. Key takeaway: occlusion culling is highly effective in occluder-rich scenes and should be baked and profiled, especially for indoor or urban environments. Occlusion Culling means bake occlusion for static scenes so unity skips hidden geometry and reduces gpu workload in complex interiors.. In practical terms, bake visibility so hidden geometry isn't rendered. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Don't draw what you can't see
keyIdea.text: Bake occlusion for static scenes so Unity skips hidden geometry and reduces GPU workload in complex interiors.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Occlusion Culling
Definition
Occlusion culling basics
Occlusion culling uses baked visibility to skip rendering objects blocked by occluders. It is computed ahead of time and consulted at runtime to avoid unnecessary draw calls and triangles.
Implementation steps
  1. Mark static occluders and occludees in the Inspector.
  2. Open Window > Rendering > Occlusion Culling and adjust settings.
  3. Click Bake and test visibility during play while profiling.
Key Takeaway

Occlusion culling can dramatically reduce render cost in scenes with many occluders, but it requires static geometry and a bake step.

Concrete Scenario
In a multi-room interior, objects behind closed doors or walls are excluded after baking, preventing unnecessary triangles from reaching the GPU when the player cannot see them.
Adjustment
Tweak smallest occluder and hole settings for accuracy versus bake time.
Common Mistake
Expecting occlusion to handle dynamic small props. The bake assumes static layout; dynamic content may need runtime culling or manual toggling.
Check
After baking, profile the GPU triangle count and verify previously hidden rooms are no longer drawn when out of view.

screens.title: Texture Atlasing & Compression
screens.subtitle: Reduce material switches and texture memory bandwidth

narration.text: Textures and materials are frequent sources of draw-call fragmentation and memory bandwidth usage. Texture atlasing combines many small textures into a single larger texture so multiple objects can share one material and texture, enabling batching. For example, several small props each with a unique texture become eligible for batching when their UVs are placed on a shared atlas. Compression reduces memory footprint and bandwidth: use desktop-friendly formats for PC and platform-specific formats like ETC or PVRTC for mobile. Lowering resolution where detail is unnecessary also saves bandwidth. A common pitfall is over-compressing or atlasing textures that need unique tiling or high detail, which can cause visible artifacts. Another issue is shader dependency: atlasing helps batching only if materials use the same shader and shader keywords. Key takeaway: atlasing and appropriate compression lower draw calls and memory use, but always test visual quality and profiling metrics on target hardware. Texture Atlasing & Compression means atlasing reduces material swaps and enables batching; compression reduces bandwidth but must preserve acceptable image quality.. In practical terms, reduce material switches and texture memory bandwidth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Share textures to batch
keyIdea.text: Atlasing reduces material swaps and enables batching; compression reduces bandwidth but must preserve acceptable image quality.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Texture Atlasing & Compression
Comparison
Atlasing vs Many Textures
Many small textures require separate material bindings and break batching. Atlasing places them into a single texture so objects can share a material and be batched together.
When to atlas
  • Many small, non-tiling textures used by similar objects.
  • UI sprites and small props that share shader behavior.
Key Takeaway

Atlasing reduces material states and enables batching; pair it with correct compression for target hardware to reduce memory bandwidth.

Concrete Example
Combine many small prop textures into a single atlas and adjust UVs so these props use one material. Measure draw-call change and texture memory in the profiler on the target device.
Atlas
Compressed
Separate
Common Mistake
Atlasing textures that require unique tiling or frequent updates creates visual artifacts or costly reuploads. Atlas only when UVs and sampling allow it.

screens.title: Shader Complexity & Simplification
screens.subtitle: Minimize shader passes and expensive operations

narration.text: Shader complexity refers to the computational cost of the shader program running per pixel or vertex. Complex shaders with multiple passes, many texture lookups, branching, or expensive lighting calculations raise G P U load. For non-critical objects, use simpler shaders like Unlit or Mobile/Diffuse to avoid extra passes. Use the Frame Debugger and the Frame Debugger's per-draw-call view to see how many passes a shader uses. A concrete example: a complex character shader with multiple layered maps can be replaced for distant characters with a cheaper variant or baked lightmaps, cutting per-pixel work. A common misconception is that a visually richer shader is always required; often a simpler shader with a well-designed atlas and baked lighting looks nearly identical at range. Key takeaway: prioritize shader simplification on objects that are numerous or dominate screen space and profile each change to confirm reduced G P U time. Shader Complexity & Simplification means replacing complex shaders with simpler alternatives or baking results can greatly cut per-pixel cost and improve frame rates.. In practical terms, minimize shader passes and expensive operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cheaper shaders save GPU
keyIdea.text: Replacing complex shaders with simpler alternatives or baking results can greatly cut per-pixel cost and improve frame rates.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Shader Complexity & Simplification
Definition
What shader complexity means
Complex shaders cost more per pixel and per vertex. Reducing passes, texture lookups, and heavy math reduces GPU time.
Strategies
  • Use simpler shaders for distant or numerous objects.
  • Avoid multiple passes unless necessary for the visual effect.
  • Bake lighting where possible instead of expensive real-time calculations.
Key Takeaway

Simpler shaders reduce per-pixel cost and often yield the largest GPU savings when applied to many objects or expensive full-screen effects.

Concrete Example
Replace a layered character shader with a single-pass mobile shader for distant NPCs, or bake their lighting into a diffuse texture to avoid per-pixel expensive operations.
Frame Debugger Tip
Use the Frame Debugger to examine shader passes for a draw call and identify high-cost draws for replacement or reduction.
Common Mistake
Assuming all visual detail must be live. Baking and cheaper shading often preserve perceived quality at much lower cost.

screens.title: Lighting & Post-processing Costs
screens.subtitle: Balance real-time light work and post effects with baking and cheaper alternatives

narration.text: Lighting and post-processing can dominate G P U cost if not carefully managed. Real-time lights with shadows are expensive per-frame, especially on many lights. Use baked lighting for static scenes where possible: baked lightmaps move expensive lighting calculations into the editor and reduce runtime G P U and C P U load. Limit the number of real-time shadow-casting lights and consider using cheaper shadow techniques or cookie textures where acceptable. Post-processing effects such as Bloom, Depth of Field, and high-quality anti-aliasing add significant overhead; on constrained hardware choose simpler options like FXAA or reduce effect resolution and sample counts. A concrete scenario: swap MSAA for FXAA and bake ambient lighting for static environment geometry to regain valuable G P U headroom. A common misstep is overusing full-screen post effects without testing their combined cost on target devices. Key takeaway: prefer baking and cheaper post-processing on limited platforms, and always test performance impact with profiling tools. In practical terms, balance real-time light work and post effects with baking and cheaper alternatives. Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Lighting & Post-processing Costs
Definition
Why lighting and post-processing matter
Real-time lights, shadows, and full-screen post effects can be expensive on the GPU. Baking lights and choosing cheaper post-processing often recovers much of the lost performance.
Strategies
  • Bake static lighting for non-dynamic scenes.
  • Limit shadow-casting real-time lights.
  • Use cheaper anti-aliasing and reduced post effect quality on mobile.
Key Takeaway

Baked lighting and judicious post-processing choices can dramatically reduce per-frame GPU cost while keeping visual quality for players.

Concrete Example
Bake global illumination for a static level and replace expensive anti-aliasing with FXAA on mobile. Measure GPU frame time before and after to confirm improvements.
Pro tip
Test lighting decisions on the target hardware; desktop tolerances differ from mobile where bandwidth and compute are constrained.
Common Mistake
Assuming a single post-processing profile is acceptable across all platforms. Tune settings per platform to maintain frame rate targets.

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through creating LOD Groups and using static batching, then verifying results with the Frame Debugger. Start with a scene that contains multiple instances of a high-polygon object. Create simplified meshes for LOD1 and LOD2, then create an empty parent GameObject named LOD_Group_Object. Add an LOD Group component and drag each mesh version into the proper LOD slots, setting transition percentages that minimize popping. Duplicate the LOD group 50 to 100 times across a large area to amplify the effect. Mark all duplicates as Static using the Inspector's Static dropdown and select Batching Static. Enter Play mode or build, then open Window, Analysis, Frame Debugger. Step through draw calls and watch how many draws represent the batched static geometry and how LODs switch as you move the camera. A common pitfall is not sharing materials across objects — if each instance uses unique materials, batching won't occur. Key takeaway: this lab shows the compound benefit of LODs plus static batching: fewer triangles and far fewer draw calls, measured live in the Frame Debugger. Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Hands-on: LOD Groups & Static Batching Lab
Lab Steps
  1. Create three mesh variants: MyObject_LOD0 (high), _LOD1 (medium), _LOD2 (low).
  2. Create an empty GameObject named LOD_Group_Object and add an LOD Group component.
  3. Assign the mesh renderers for each LOD slot and tune transition percentages.
  4. Duplicate the LOD_Group_Object 50–100 times to populate the scene.
  5. Select all duplicates and mark them Static > Batching Static in the Inspector.
  6. Run Play mode, open Window > Analysis > Frame Debugger, and step through draw calls to confirm batching and LOD switching.
Verification
Observe draw-call reduction and LOD swaps. Also check memory for increased combined mesh buffers when using static batching.
Example Inspector Checklist
// Steps in words: add LOD Group, assign renderers, set transitions, mark objects Static for batching.
Expected Result
Triangle count drops as LODs switch and draw calls fall drastically when static batching combines geometry.
Common Mistake
Using different materials per instance prevents batching. Ensure shared materials when batching is intended.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the core ideas to remember. First, a draw call is a C P U instruction to the G P U; when the render thread is heavy, reduce draw calls. Second, batching and instancing are complementary: static batching combines immobile meshes at edit time; dynamic batching merges small meshes at runtime; G P U instancing lets the G P U render many identical copies efficiently. Third, LOD groups reduce triangle throughput by swapping lower-detail meshes at distance. Fourth, occlusion culling prevents rendering of geometry hidden by occluders when baked for static scenes. Fifth, texture atlasing and compression reduce material state changes and memory bandwidth. Finally, simplify shaders and prefer baked lighting or cheaper post-processing when targeting constrained hardware. Each of these strategies should be applied and then verified with the Frame Debugger and Profiler to confirm a net improvement.

keyIdea.title: Apply + Verify
keyIdea.text: Use batching, instancing, LOD, occlusion, and texture strategies, then profile to confirm gains.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Key Concepts
Draw Call
A CPU command to render geometry. Reduce count to lower render-thread overhead.
Batching & Instancing
Static batching for immobile objects, dynamic batching for small runtime objects, and instancing for many identical meshes.
LOD Groups
Swap lower-detail meshes by distance to reduce triangles without harming distant visual quality.
Takeaway
Combine these techniques thoughtfully and always measure with the Frame Debugger and Profiler to ensure each change helps your target platform.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Continued
screens.subtitle: Short reminders for practice and profiling

narration.text: A few quick reminders: atlasing and compression reduce texture bandwidth and allow shared materials for batching. Simplify shaders and bake lighting for static content. Use occlusion culling in occluder-rich scenes to skip hidden geometry. Always compare changes on your target hardware and use the Frame Debugger to inspect draw calls and shader passes. Finally, remember that optimization is iterative: change one thing, profile, and confirm. If a change does not reduce frame time on your target device, revert or try a different approach. This workflow prevents wasted time and ensures your optimizations produce real results. Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Key Concepts — Continued
Texture Optimization
Atlas, compress, and scale textures per-platform to reduce bandwidth and allow batching.
Avoid Overuse
Do not overuse real-time lights or heavy post effects without profiling — they can quickly overwhelm the GPU.
Profile Often
Use Frame Debugger and Profiler after each change. Metrics and visuals both matter for a balanced result.
Final Tip
Optimization is a measurement-driven craft. One change at a time and test on the hardware your players use.
